post.caption: Van Cleef's jewels became a ballet. Jeweler Claude Arpels gave choreographer George Balanchine the idea for a ballet about gems. In early 1966, Balanchine visited Van Cleef and Arpels' Fifth Avenue salons, and the jewels there struck him. The ballet has three parts, Emeralds, then Rubies, then Diamonds, and the music runs from Faure to Stravinsky to Tchaikovsky. A part for sapphires was planned, then dropped. Balanchine said the dancers are just dressed like jewels. It is often called the first full length abstract ballet and premiered on April 13, 1967, at the New York State Theater.
